design_detail: Systematic review of published case reports (18), case series (10) and conference abstracts (4) describing eye problems after recreational use of poppers (alkyl nitrites; the paper writes 'nitrate' throughout), published 2004-2021: 113 patients. Patient-level data pooled descriptively in SPSS, with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of visual acuity (logMAR) from presentation to follow-up and a Kruskal-Wallis test across follow-up times; reports appraised with JBI checklists (case reports and series) or AACODS (abstracts), converted to scores. The authors call it a systematic review and meta-analysis; there is no meta-analysis of effect estimates. Read as the online-first PDF (a cover page, then article pages 1-9); printed later as Semin Ophthalmol 2023;38(4):371-379, so page numbers here are those of the online-first PDF.
can_establish: What has been published about people who developed eye problems after using poppers: their symptoms and eye findings at presentation, how often follow-up was reported, and how vision and retinal scans changed in those who were followed up.
cannot_establish: How often poppers cause eye problems (no count of people who use poppers); that poppers caused each case (uncontrolled reports; other causes such as bright-light exposure are discussed); which product, amount or pattern of use carries the risk (compound unknown for 89% and patterns not analysable); or whether stopping poppers or taking lutein helps (no comparison, and stopping was documented for 27 people).

sample.recruitment: Published reports from CINAHL, Embase and PubMed searched on 27 November 2021, plus Google Scholar for grey literature; English language and human subjects only (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Case reports, series and conference abstracts of people diagnosed with maculopathy, or with at least one anatomical or functional eye anomaly, attributed to recreational alkyl nitrite use; excluded: pre-existing eye conditions that could affect outcomes; no age limit (p. 2). Of 45 full texts, 13 were excluded: missing outcome 10, diagnosis 1, non-English 1, design 1 (Figure 1, p. 3).
sample.demographics: 108 men (95.6%) and 5 women; mean age 40.16 (SD 9.49; range 13-64); HIV status unknown for 92 (81.4%), positive for 19 (16.8%), negative for 2 (p. 2). More than half of the patients were reported from the UK (p. 2; Table 1, p. 4).
sample.attrition: Within the pooled data, follow-up acuity exists for 40 of the 69 patients with acuity at presentation, follow-up OCT for 75 of 111, follow-up time for 49 of 113, and treatment for 45 (pp. 3-5).
sample.selection_effects: Published cases only: reports favour striking, unusual or well-imaged cases. Several UK series come from overlapping author groups (for example Finnerty 2016 and Hughes 2017 share authors), so the same patients may be counted twice; the review does not check this. English only.

exposure.measurement: Poppers use as described in each report; the compound was not reported for 100 patients (88.5%); of the 13 with a compound, 9 used isopropyl nitrite, 1 amyl, 1 isobutyl and 2 mixtures (p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported: inhalation; patterns from a single episode (in several reports 12 to 48 hours before presentation) to regular use for more than 20 years (p. 3; Table 1, p. 4); amounts not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Not analysed; the authors mention possible added effects of syphilis, antiretroviral therapy and other drugs (p. 6).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. At follow-up, whether people had stopped poppers was documented for 27 patients, 19 of whom had (p. 3).

comparison.controls: None; before-and-after comparison within patients who had follow-up.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Vision before poppers use, exposure to bright light (sun or club lighting, discussed as an alternative cause, p. 7), other eye or general disease, HIV and its treatment, and other drug use.

outcomes.instruments: Snellen acuity converted to logMAR; fundoscopy; spectral-domain OCT; full-field and multifocal electroretinogram; fundus autofluorescence; fluorescein angiography; visual fields; intraocular pressure (pp. 4-6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Tests and their timing varied between reports; anatomical findings were extracted per patient because per-eye data were not available, acuity per eye (p. 5).
outcomes.operationalization: Poppers maculopathy as diagnosed by each report's authors; improvement as lower logMAR, or as scan findings reported as improved or resolved.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five tests: one overall Wilcoxon test, one for each of three follow-up periods, and one Kruskal-Wallis test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; clinicians reporting their own patients.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive proportions and logMAR means. Acuity at presentation: mean 0.22 (SD 0.19; range −0.1 to 1.3), 136 eyes of 69 patients. In the 79 eyes of 40 patients with follow-up: 0.24 to 0.11 (Wilcoxon Z = −5.800, p < 0.001); 1-2 months 0.24 to 0.12 (Z = −3.596), 3-6 months 0.22 to 0.12 (Z = −3.501), more than 6 months 0.25 to 0.08 (Z = −3.095, p = .002); no difference between follow-up periods (Kruskal-Wallis p > .05). Best eye at presentation: −0.1 to 0.5, mean 0.18; 9 of 69 best eyes (13%) at 0.4 logMAR or worse, of whom 2 were followed up, unchanged. OCT improved or resolved in 46 of 75 with follow-up (61.3%).
analysis.selective_reporting: What could be pooled depended on what each report published: presentation details for 69, complaint for 56, treatment for 45 and follow-up time for 49 of 113 patients.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Published cases of eye problems after poppers mostly concern men with both eyes affected, a mild loss of acuity or visual disturbances, a yellow spot at the fovea and disruption of the photoreceptor (ellipsoid) layer on OCT. Among the minority followed up, acuity and scans mostly improved; follow-up was selective, and whether stopping poppers helps could not be judged.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that patients 'have a good visual prognosis', with stopping poppers potentially playing a role (p. 1); the Conclusion says recreational use 'can cause vision loss and foveal damage' (p. 8). The Discussion infers that one patient had stopped because his vision improved, and supports a role for stopping with the 93% advised to stop, a share of the 45 with treatment documented (p. 7). The authors' own Limitations say uncontrolled reports cannot support robust associations (p. 8).

timeline.event: Pece et al., the first report of eye problems linked to poppers (as described on p. 1).
Davies et al., UK case series that named poppers maculopathy (included).
Van Bol et al., UK case series describing three clinical phenotypes (included; 42 patients in Table 1, 39 in the Discussion).
González-Martín-Moro et al., a quantitative review of the earlier literature on poppers maculopathy, cited in the Discussion (p. 6) but not compared.

replication.where_it_stands: The evidence remains case reports and series. The review presents itself as the first systematic review, yet cites an earlier quantitative review of the same literature (González-Martín-Moro 2021) without comparing results. No cohort of people who use poppers with eye examinations was found by the review.

funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest reported (p. 8).
funding.affiliations_note: Discipline of Orthoptics, La Trobe University, Melbourne.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people who use poppers, examined with OCT over time and recording the products used (tested by drug checking) and how often they are used, would show how often maculopathy occurs and with what; follow-up of diagnosed cases with and without continued use would show whether stopping helps recovery.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People with eye anomalies after poppers, exposure, outcomes (acuity, signs) stated; no comparator by design.

domains.domain: 2. Protocol registered before the review (critical)
domains.note: None reported.

domains.domain: 3. Explanation of study designs included
domains.note: Only case reports, series and abstracts were sought; no reason is given.

domains.domain: 4. Comprehensive literature search (critical)
domains.note: Three databases and Google Scholar with search terms listed, but limited to English without justification (one eligible report excluded for language); no reference-list or expert search described.

domains.domain: 5. Study selection in duplicate
domains.note: Titles and abstracts were screened independently, but the reviewers and the agreement process are not stated, and full-text selection is not described as duplicate.

domains.domain: 6. Data extraction in duplicate
domains.note: Customised Excel form; duplicate extraction not stated.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only counts by reason in the flow diagram (p. 3).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, country, sex and age, pattern of use, compound and appraisal score; follow-up and outcomes per report are not tabulated.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: JBI checklists and AACODS by two reviewers independently, but summed into scores without item-level results; one report (Pece 2004) has no score.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

domains.domain: 11. Appropriate statistical methods for meta-analysis (critical)
domains.note: Pooled before-after tests treat 79 eyes of 40 patients from many reports as independent observations and use only the patients who were followed up.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis by report quality.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations acknowledge uncontrolled designs, but the abstract and Conclusion state a good prognosis and a causal effect.

domains.domain: 14. Heterogeneity explained and discussed
domains.note: Differences in testing and follow-up noted only as a limitation; only follow-up time was examined.

domains.domain: 15. Publication bias investigated (critical)
domains.note: Not considered, although which cases get published is the main selection problem in a review of case reports.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding; no conflicts declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Several critical items fail (no protocol, an unjustified English-only search, no list of exclusions, inappropriate pooling, causal and prognostic conclusions beyond the data, publication bias not considered), giving critically low confidence by AMSTAR 2. The review is still a useful, transparent collection of the published cases: it can be cited for what reported cases looked like at presentation and for the share of followed-up cases that improved. It cannot be cited for how often poppers damage the eyes, for causation, for prognosis in all cases, or for any effect of stopping or of lutein.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 122 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1-9 of the online-first version (PDFs/Alkyl-nitrites-and-inhalants/Bartolo_2023_PoppersMaculopathySR..pdf: a cover page, then the article numbered 1-9; published online 7 August 2022, printed as Semin Ophthalmol 2023;38(4):371-379), read in full including Tables 1-5, the PRISMA flow chart, the Figure 2 caption, funding, disclosure and reference list; extracted once with pdftotext; Table 1 and the acuity paragraphs (pp. 1, 4, 7) checked on 110 dpi renderings, including every negative value.

key_findings.finding: Search on 27 November 2021 (PubMed 392, EMBASE 81, CINAHL 18, Google Scholar 2 records): 493 records, 65 duplicates, 428 screened, 45 full texts, 32 included (18 case reports, 10 case series, 4 conference abstracts), published 2004-2021.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategy (p. 2); Results › Search Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Figure 1 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: 113 patients: 108 men (95.6%) and 5 women (4.4%), mean age 40.16 (SD 9.49; range 13-64); HIV status unknown for 92 (81.4%), positive for nineteen (16.8%), negative for 2 (1.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Patient Demographics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 1 adds up to 116 patients and 6 women (editors' count; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Use ranged from a single episode to chronic use for more than 20 years; the compound was not reported for 100 patients (88.5%); the influence of use on outcomes could not be analysed because reporting varied.
key_findings.locator: Results › Popper Usage, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Presentation known for 69: both eyes in 67 (97.1%), one eye in 2. Complaint known for 56, with 81 complaints in all: changes in acuity 36 (44.4%), visual disturbances such as phosphenes, flashes and distortion 29 (35.7%), central scotoma 15 (18.5%), pain behind the eye 1 (1.2%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical Presentation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Table 2 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Visual acuity: 136 eyes of 69 patients at presentation, mean 0.22 logMAR (about 6/9.5; SD 0.19; range −0.1 to 1.3). In the 79 eyes of 40 patients with follow-up, mean 0.24 (SD 0.19) improved to 0.11 (about 6/7.5; SD 0.17; range −0.3 to 0.5), Wilcoxon Z = −5.800, p < 0.001; improvement at 1-2 months (36 eyes, 0.24 to 0.12, Z = −3.596), 3-6 months (24 eyes, 0.22 to 0.12, Z = −3.501) and over 6 months (19 eyes, 0.25 to 0.08, Z = −3.095, p = .002), with no difference between periods (p > .05).
key_findings.locator: Results › Visual Acuity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Best eye: at presentation −0.1 (6/5) to 0.5 (6/19), mean 0.18 (SD 0.15), 69 eyes; at follow-up −0.3 to 0.5, mean 0.09 (SD 0.16), 32 eyes. 87% of best eyes had good vision, but 9 (13%) were at 0.4 logMAR (6/15) or worse; only 2 of these were followed up and their vision was unchanged, so the effect of treatment or of stopping poppers on acuity could not be analysed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Visual Acuity, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fundoscopy at presentation in 72 patients: bilateral yellow foveal spot in 53 (73.6%; alone in 50, with foveal irregularity in 2, with optic disc blurring in 1), foveal irregularity alone 3, normal 11 (15.2%). At follow-up 14 patients, 4 (28.6%) normal, all at 1-2 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Anatomical Changes, 2nd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: OCT at presentation in 111 patients: disturbance of the sub-foveal ellipsoid layer 89 (80.1%), vitelliform-like lesion 14 (12.7%), micro-hole 4, full-thickness macular hole 1, normal 3. At follow-up (75 patients): unchanged 29, improved 22, resolved 24, so improved or resolved 46 (61.3%); by time, 10 of 19 at 1-2 months (52.6%), 9 of 13 at 3-6 months (69.2%), 8 of 9 later (88.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Anatomical Changes, 3rd paragraph (starts on p. 5); Table 4

key_findings.finding: Treatment documented for 45 patients (39.8%): stopping poppers for 42 (93%), 3 of whom were also given oral lutein; lutein alone for 2; vitrectomy for 1. Compliance documented for 27, of whom 19 (70.3%) were compliant at follow-up. Follow-up time reported for 49 (43%): 1-3 months 25, 4-6 months 13, 7-12 months 5, 13-16 months 3, 17-48 months 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment and Follow-up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The two patients with the longest follow-up: patient A, reported as not stopping, had acuity 0.2 in both eyes at presentation and at 40-42 months; patient B improved from 0.2 and 0.5 to −0.1 in both eyes at 46-48 months, with no mention of whether he stopped. Some earlier series reported no improvement and no resolution within 3 months despite stopping.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Visual Acuity, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Prognosis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Full-field ERG in 7 at presentation (5 normal); multifocal ERG in 8 (6 with reduced central responses); autofluorescence in 36 (normal 20, increased peri-foveal 9, reduced 7); fluorescein angiography in 17 (normal 12); visual fields in 18 (normal 14); anterior segment (24) and eye pressure (20) normal.
key_findings.locator: Results › Anatomical Changes, 4th and 5th paragraphs (pp. 5-6); Table 5 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: case reports and series are uncontrolled and can suggest hypotheses but not robust associations; data sets inconsistent, missing data, varied testing and follow-up; prospective studies of outcomes and treatment are needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists 116 patients (editors' count), with Van Bol et al. (2017) as 37 men and 5 women, while the text gives 113 patients (p. 2) and the Discussion describes Van Bol's series as 39 patients (p. 7); Table 1 also lists 6 women (Van Bol 5, Catala-Mora 1) against 5 in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Denominators are uncertain by a few patients; the totals are used as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The age range in the text is 13-64 (p. 2), but Table 1 includes patients up to 70 (Van Bol et al., 27-70) (p. 4).
Four of 56 patients with three complaints are printed as 35.7%; 4 of 56 is 7.1% (editors' calculation).
Compliance documented for 27 patients is printed as 15%; 27 of 113 is 24%, 27 of 45 is 60% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: How many patients were known to have stopped is smaller than the 93% figure suggests: 19 confirmed of 113.

reporting_issues.issue: The three acuity follow-up groups are labelled group 1, group 2 and group 2; the second group's baseline SD of 0.45 for 24 eyes is incompatible with an SD of 0.19 for all 79 eyes (a subgroup of 24 with SD 0.45 implies an overall SD of at least 0.24, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the acuity summaries is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The OCT follow-up groups (19 + 13 + 9 = 41) do not add up to the 49 patients with follow-up time, and the last group is described as greater than 3 months, overlapping the 3-6 month group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The improvement by time after presentation is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The before-after Wilcoxon tests treat 79 eyes of 40 patients as independent observations (p. 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The p values overstate the precision of the improvement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the work a meta-analysis and the Introduction says no systematic review had been published (p. 1), but the Discussion cites a 2021 quantitative review of the same literature (González-Martín-Moro et al., p. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's novelty is overstated and the two reviews are not compared.

reporting_issues.issue: The compounds are called alkyl nitrates throughout, while the titles of several cited references name them nitrites (references 1, 3, 8, 13 and 54).
reporting_issues.consequence: Naming error; poppers are alkyl nitrites.

reporting_issues.issue: Hughes et al. 2017 (reference 37, an included series) and Rewbury et al. 2017 (reference 53) have the same title and citation (Br J Ophthalmol 2017;101(11):1530-1534), with the authors in a different order.
reporting_issues.consequence: The same article is cited twice; a check for patients counted twice is all the more needed.

reporting_issues.issue: Pece et al. 2004 has no appraisal score in Table 1.

design_detail: Case series of 110 sudden deaths of young people in the United States after sniffing volatile hydrocarbons, excluding deaths by plastic-bag suffocation, during the 1960s (1962 to 1 April 1969 in the Figure 1 legend). The deaths were gathered by a nationwide survey in the winter and spring of 1969, which followed a telephone survey of East Coast medical examiner offices after the author learned of one such death in the summer of 1968; who was surveyed, how cases were defined and attributed, and how many offices replied are not reported. The paper abridges the author's DSc thesis in forensic medicine (Johns Hopkins School of Hygiene and Public Health). It reports six eyewitness accounts, the deaths by region and chemical (Figure 2), a table of activities or stresses in 18 deaths, autopsy and toxicology findings, demographics, concealment of sniffing by families or friends, and a proposed mechanism (cardiac arrhythmia from light anaesthesia, made worse by raised carbon dioxide, stress or activity) drawn from animal and anaesthesia studies.
can_establish: That in the 1960s sudden deaths without suffocation and, where autopsied, without an anatomical cause were being reported among young people in the United States after sniffing volatile hydrocarbons, mostly aerosol fluorocarbon propellants and 1,1,1-trichloroethane; that witnesses in several of these deaths described sudden running, panic or exertion just before collapse; and that sniffing was concealed by families or friends in some deaths.
cannot_establish: How often sniffing ends in sudden death or whether the rate rose (no denominators; cases found by a 1969 survey whose methods and completeness are not described); that exertion, fright or stress raises the risk (no comparison with sniffing episodes that did not end in death, and an activity is recorded for only 18 of 110 deaths); or the mechanism (no heart rhythm was recorded in any case; arrhythmia is inferred from negative autopsies and from animal and anaesthesia studies).

sample.recruitment: Deaths identified by a nationwide survey in the winter and spring of 1969, preceded by a telephone survey of East Coast medical examiner offices (p. 2075, Background, 3rd paragraph). The survey's respondents, questions, case definition and response rate are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Sudden deaths of young people associated with sniffing volatile hydrocarbons, excluding deaths by plastic-bag suffocation (abstract and Figure 1 legend). No formal case definition, no stated criteria for attributing a death to sniffing, and no stated period beyond 'the 1960's' (abstract) and 1962 to 1 April 1969 (Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Ages 11 to 23; 105 described as of European ancestry and 5 others (one Mexican, one Puerto Rican, one American Indian and two Black youths, in the paper's terms); 13 white girls or young women (the sex of the 5 others is not stated); 81 from middle-income suburban homes; 37 with a history of occasional or habitual sniffing (p. 2079). Deaths by region: West 57, Central 18, East 35 (Figure 2, p. 2077).
sample.selection_effects: Cases are those known to the offices reached by the survey and recorded or remembered by them in 1969. The study began with East Coast cases, and the last period (1968 to April 1969) is one combined bin, so recent cases and areas with active medical examiner systems are likely over-represented. Deaths with plastic-bag suffocation were excluded by design, and deaths in which sniffing was concealed and never uncovered would be missing (sniffing was concealed in 8 of the identified deaths).

exposure.measurement: Chemical assignment procedures are not described. Volatile hydrocarbons were reported on toxicological examination of organs in 44 autopsied deaths and quantified in 12 (p.2079); the number tested and how chemical groups were assigned in the remaining cases are not stated.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not quantified. 37 of the 110 had a history of occasional or habitual sniffing, one for over four years (p. 2079).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: no information on alcohol or other drugs in the toxicology.

comparison.controls: None: no comparison with sniffing episodes that did not end in death, or with other sudden deaths.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: At necropsy no anatomical abnormality explained the deaths, and review of autopsy protocols and slides showed no endocrine disorder; previous medical history showed one person with grand mal seizures and two with bronchial asthma (p. 2079). Other drugs, ambient conditions and time from sniffing to death are not reported for the series.

outcomes.instruments: Autopsy and review of autopsy protocols and available slides; toxicological examination of organs (methods not described) (p. 2079). In the eyewitness accounts, a complete autopsy is reported in five of six (pp. 2075–2076). The total number of autopsies and of toxicology analyses is not given.
outcomes.validity_norms: No stated criteria for attributing death to sniffing. Eight of the 12 quantified levels are described as compatible with light plane anaesthesia of similar hydrocarbon anaesthetics, without the values, the specimen, the method or the reference used (p. 2079).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Sudden sniffing death': sudden, almost instantaneous death after sniffing a volatile hydrocarbon, without plastic-bag suffocation and, where an autopsy was done, without an anatomical cause.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts only; no rates. By region (Figure 2, printed in the figure): West 57, Central 18, East 35. By chemical (editors' sums of the regional figures): aerosol fluorocarbon propellants, with or without trichloroethane, 59; 1,1,1-trichloroethane 29; toluene 8; benzene 7; gasoline 4; toluene with trichloroethane 2; unidentified hydrocarbon 1; total 110. The yearly panels of Figure 2 (read from the figure, approximate) show the largest counts for fluorocarbon propellants, trichloroethane, toluene and gasoline in the combined 1968–1969 bin; benzene instead peaks around 3 in 1967 and falls to about 1 in the final bin. Trichloroethane has up to about 3 in 1964. The fluorocarbon panel is marked at 49 for the final bin. Activity or stress listed for 18 deaths (Table, p. 2078). Editors' calculation: 18 of 110 is 16%; volatile hydrocarbons were found at toxicology in 44 (40% of the series; the number autopsied is not given).
analysis.selective_reporting: Survey methods, the number of autopsies and toxicology analyses, and the measured concentrations are not reported; only six eyewitness accounts are described, chosen without a stated rule.

interpretation_gap.results_show: 110 sudden deaths of young people after sniffing volatile hydrocarbons, mainly aerosol propellants (59) and trichloroethane (29), found through a 1969 survey; no anatomical cause where an autopsy is described; sudden running, panic or exertion before collapse in several witnessed deaths; an activity or stress listed for 18; volatile hydrocarbons found at toxicology in 44 and quantified in 12; sniffing concealed by family or friends in 8.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the epidemic "appears to have originated on the West Coast", that "The incidence rate showed a sharp rise" in the late 1960 s, that deaths showed a preponderance in suburban middle-income white families, and that arrhythmia from light anaesthesia, made worse by raised carbon dioxide, stress or activity, is "the most likely explanation for sniffing death" (p. 2075). Gaps: (1) no incidence rate was computed (there is no population or count of people who sniff), and a rise in counts found by a 1969 survey, with a combined 1968–1969 bin, may reflect recall and ascertainment; (2) the West Coast origin and the social and ethnic preponderance have no denominators; (3) arrhythmia was not recorded in any case: it is inferred from negative autopsies and from cat and anaesthesia studies, and the Comment itself says it is difficult to say whether the terminal event accompanied by panic reflected arrhythmia with pulmonary oedema, light anaesthesia, a hyperadrenergic crisis or other factors (p. 2079); (4) the role of exertion and stress rests on 18 listed deaths and 8 accounts of a sudden dash, with no comparison group.

timeline.event: Hall and Hine: two deaths associated with trichloroethane in San Francisco within six weeks, attributed by them to chemical pneumonia and respiratory arrest, as described in this paper (p. 2078).
Press and Done: 12 United States fatalities attributed to solvent sniffing, 8 of them to bag suffocation and 4 not meeting the criteria of sudden sniffing death, as described in this paper (p. 2078).
Baselt and Carvey: sudden sniffing death of a 15-year-old boy involving two fluorocarbon propellants, as described in this paper (p. 2078).
Darke et al. (2023): circumstances of solvent deaths in Australia, noted on the project's reading list as a later death series; not listed and not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no later death series was read for this card. The paper is the landmark description named on the project's list for deaths after exertion or fright during solvent inhalation; its observations are descriptive, its counts are not rates, and its mechanism is a proposal from other studies.

funding.funder: Public Health Service research grant ST-1-GM-1218 (p. 2079).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Division of Forensic Pathology, Johns Hopkins School of Hygiene and Public Health, and the Maryland Medical Legal Foundation, Inc., Baltimore; the article abridges the author's DSc thesis in forensic medicine (p. 2075).

what_would_settle_it: For frequency: population-based death registers with a stated case definition and toxicology in every suspected death, set against estimates of how many people inhale volatile substances. For the role of exertion or fright: a comparison of circumstances between fatal and non-fatal inhalation episodes (case-control or case-crossover). For the mechanism: recorded heart rhythms in people resuscitated after collapse, and studies relating measured post-mortem concentrations to those that sensitize the heart in experiments.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The offices reached by an undescribed 1969 survey are not a frame for all such deaths in the United States.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately
domains.note: How deaths were identified, reported and selected is not described.

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size
domains.note: 110 deaths are enough to describe a pattern; no frequency is estimated.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age range, ethnicity, region, social background and chemical are given for the series, but there is no case table, and circumstances are described only for 6 eyewitness accounts and 18 listed activities.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: The numbers autopsied and tested are not given; activity is recorded for 18 of 110; the yearly panels do not appear to add up to the regional totals for benzene and trichloroethane (approximate reading).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: No stated case definition or attribution criteria. Positive organ toxicology is reported for 44 deaths, but numbers autopsied/tested and classification procedures for other cases are not reported.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Different offices with different practices; toxicology methods unstated; concentrations measured in 12 and not reported.

domains.domain: 8. Appropriate statistical analysis
domains.note: Counts suit a description, but a rising incidence is asserted without any denominator.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: How many offices were surveyed and replied is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI checklist, as the round brief directs for case series without a comparison. The series is large for its time and its clinical observations are vivid, but it was assembled by an undescribed survey, without a case definition, denominators, a complete record of autopsy and toxicology, or any comparison, so the editors summarise the risk of bias as high for anything beyond description. It may be cited for the existence and character of sudden deaths after inhaling volatile hydrocarbons in the 1960s, the products and chemicals involved in the reported deaths, the witnessed sudden running or panic before collapse, the negative autopsies, and the concealment of sniffing; not for rates, trends, risk factors or mechanism.

key_findings.finding: The series comprises 110 sudden deaths of young Americans after sniffing volatile hydrocarbons, without plastic-bag suffocation, during the 1960s, gathered by a nationwide survey in the winter and spring of 1969 after a telephone survey of East Coast medical examiner offices; the survey's methods are not described.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Background, 3rd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Figure 2 prints the deaths by region and chemical: West 57 (aerosol 36, trichloroethane 9, toluene 6, gasoline 3, benzene 1, unidentified 1, toluene with trichloroethane 1), Central 18 (aerosol 10, benzene 4, trichloroethane 3, gasoline 1) and East 35 (trichloroethane 17, aerosol 13, benzene 2, toluene 2, toluene with trichloroethane 1). Editors' sums: aerosol fluorocarbon propellants (with or without trichloroethane) 59, 1,1,1-trichloroethane 29, toluene 8, benzene 7, gasoline 4, toluene with trichloroethane 2, unidentified 1.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2, map (top)
key_findings.note: Printed in the figure, which is an image; the numbers are not in the PDF's text layer and were read on 150-dpi and 300-dpi renderings.

key_findings.finding: The yearly panels of Figure 2 have their largest counts in the combined 1968–early 1969 bin for fluorocarbon propellants (marked 49), trichloroethane, toluene (about 6) and gasoline, but benzene peaks in 1967 (about 3) and falls to about 1 in the final bin. Earlier trichloroethane counts reach about 3 in 1964.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2, yearly panels (bottom)
key_findings.note: Approximate readings from the original Figure 2 rendered at 300 dpi; plotted points do not always sit on whole numbers. The combined 1968–1969 bin extends to 1 April 1969 (Figure 1 caption,p.2076), about 15 months. Apparent panel sums are about 6 benzene versus 7 in the map, about 26 trichloroethane versus 29, and about 58 fluorocarbon propellants versus 59. The article does not explain these discrepancies.

key_findings.finding: Six eyewitness accounts (five boys and one girl, aged 15 to 17; products a hair-shampoo aerosol, an antitussive aerosol, cleaning fluid in two, a frying-pan aerosol and airplane glue): in five the person suddenly ran, screamed or became agitated before collapsing, and in the sixth he called out that his heart was stopping before collapsing; five were dead on arrival at hospital and one was found dead; complete autopsy in five showed no anatomical cause of death, and one had no autopsy.
key_findings.locator: Eyewitness Reports on SSD, cases 1 to 6

key_findings.finding: Activities or stresses associated with sudden death, listed for 18 deaths: wrestling or scuffling after sniffing 3; caught by police, then running 2; autoerotic activity 2; surprised by parents or police 2; riding a bicycle 2; walking in snow or very cold weather 2; a hallucinogenic crisis 2; dancing, then sniffing 1; throwing a heavy weight 1; singing 1.
key_findings.locator: Table (Activity or Stress Associated With Sudden Death)
key_findings.note: No comparison: how often the same activities occurred in sniffing episodes that did not end in death is unknown.

key_findings.finding: In eight witnessed deaths the person suddenly dashed a few hundred feet and then collapsed; the author says it is difficult to say whether the terminal event accompanied by panic reflected arrhythmia with pulmonary oedema, the excitement of light anaesthesia, a hyperadrenergic crisis or a combination with other unknown factors.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 13th paragraph (last on p. 2078, continuing on p. 2079)
key_findings.note: The total number of witnessed deaths is not stated, nor whether these eight overlap with the Table's 18.

key_findings.finding: At necropsy no anatomical abnormality explained the deaths, and review of autopsy protocols and slides found no endocrine disorder; medical histories showed one person with grand mal seizures and two with bronchial asthma. Toxicological examination of the organs found volatile hydrocarbons in 44 autopsied deaths; in the 12 with quantitative results, 8 were said to have levels compatible with light plane anaesthesia of similar hydrocarbon anaesthetics.
key_findings.locator: Comment, end of the 14th paragraph and the 15th paragraph (p. 2079, left column)
key_findings.note: The number autopsied and the number tested are not given, and no concentrations, specimens or methods are reported, so 'compatible with light anaesthesia' cannot be checked.

key_findings.finding: Decedents were aged 11 to 23; 105 were described as of European ancestry and 5 were not; 13 were white girls or young women; 81 came from middle-income suburban homes; 37 had a history of occasional or habitual sniffing.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 15th and 16th paragraphs (p. 2079, left column, continuing in the middle column)

key_findings.finding: In 8 deaths family or friends withheld information about the sniffing: in one an older brother came forward hours after the death, in one family and friends gave a fabricated account, and in six the concealment of information or of sniffing materials was uncovered by police investigation; the author credits the persistence of coroner and police.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 17th paragraph (p. 2079, middle column)
key_findings.note: Bears on undercounting: deaths in which sniffing stayed hidden would not have entered the series.

key_findings.finding: Products considered of low toxicity on the basis of human and animal experiments were associated with these deaths: the aerosol propellants (trichlorofluoromethane, dichlorodifluoromethane, cryofluorane) had shown very low toxicity in acute inhalation tests in rats and guinea pigs, and trichloroethane was regarded as one of the least toxic chlorinated solvents.
key_findings.locator: Background, 3rd paragraph (p. 2075); Comment, 2nd, 3rd and 7th paragraphs (p. 2078)

key_findings.finding: The proposed mechanism (catecholamines released by activity or stress, and raised carbon dioxide from bag use, sensitizing the heart to hydrocarbons and causing sudden arrhythmia) is supported by cited cat, Purkinje-fibre and anaesthesia studies; no heart rhythm was recorded in any of the deaths.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 10th to 12th paragraphs (p. 2078, right column) and 14th paragraph (p. 2079)

reporting_issues.issue: The survey that produced the 110 deaths is described only as a nationwide survey in the winter and spring of 1969: who was asked, the case definition, how deaths were attributed to sniffing and how many offices replied are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Completeness and representativeness are unknown; the counts are a minimum of reported cases, not a census.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract speaks of a sharply rising incidence rate, but no rate is computed anywhere (no population or number of people sniffing), and the last bin of the yearly panels combines 1968 with early 1969.
reporting_issues.consequence: No rate or trend can be cited from this paper; the rise in counts cannot be separated from the timing and method of the survey.

reporting_issues.issue: The yearly panels of Figure 2 appear inconsistent with its regional totals for benzene (about 6 versus 7), trichloroethane (about 26 versus 29) and fluorocarbon propellants (about 58 versus 59); annual points are approximate graphical readings.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source does not explain the discrepancies; missing years, plotting error and other explanations cannot be distinguished. Do not substitute a reconstructed exact annual count or infer an incidence trend.

reporting_issues.issue: Volatile hydrocarbons were found 'in 44 of the autopsied patients', but the number autopsied and the number tested are not given, and none of the 12 quantitative results is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Positive organ toxicology is reported for 44 of 110 deaths, with the numbers autopsied and tested unstated; how the remaining cases were assigned is not reported. This does not establish that they were untested or were attributed from circumstances. The unreported quantitative values cannot be checked against the author's anaesthetic-range judgment.

reporting_issues.issue: The total number of witnessed deaths is not stated; eight are said to have involved a sudden dash, and the Table lists 18 deaths with an activity or stress, without saying how the two groups overlap.
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of deaths preceded by exertion or fright cannot be computed; '18 of 110' is a lower bound of recorded circumstances, not a frequency.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites 'Press and Dome' where the reference list has Press E, Done AK; and the sex of the five decedents not of European ancestry is not stated, so the number of girls and young women is 13 or more.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract says the epidemic "appears to have originated on the West Coast", that "The incidence rate showed a sharp rise" in the late 1960s, that deaths showed a preponderance in suburban middle-income white families, and that arrhythmia from light anaesthesia, made worse by raised carbon dioxide, stress or activity, is "the most likely explanation for sniffing death" (p. 2075). Gaps: (1) no incidence rate was computed (there is no population or count of people who sniff), and a rise in counts found by a 1969 survey, with a combined 1968–1969 bin, may reflect recall and ascertainment; (2) the West Coast origin and the social and ethnic preponderance have no denominators; (3) arrhythmia was not recorded in any case: it is inferred from negative autopsies and from cat and anaesthesia studies, and the Comment itself says it is difficult to say whether the terminal panic reflected arrhythmia with pulmonary oedema, light anaesthesia, a hyperadrenergic crisis or other factors (p. 2079); (4) the role of exertion and stress rests on 18 listed deaths and 8 accounts of a sudden dash, with no comparison group.
